Washoe County at a glance

Washoe County occupies Nevada's northwest corner, and its seat is Reno. At the 2020 census it held 486,492 people, making it the state's second most populous county. Reno and Sparks are the only incorporated cities. Incline Village, Sun Valley, Spanish Springs, Verdi, Gerlach and the rest are unincorporated. A single Treasurer bills every parcel, so a downtown Reno bungalow and a Lake Tahoe cabin go through the same office even though their tax districts differ.

The Assessor posts tax district maps and neighborhood maps, along with Sales Reports, a Median Sales Chart and Current Statistical Reports. Check recorded sales near you there before judging any offer.

Wildfire, flood and permit questions

Fire is the chief natural hazard, concentrated in southern Reno and just beyond the city limits. Southwest Reno fires have moved quickly, the 2011 Caughlin Fire among them, and construction keeps pushing into forested ground. Lenders and insurers sometimes ask if a parcel lies in a FEMA floodplain; the Assessor's office answers that and can provide elevation certificates.

  • Put known fire damage, burn scars or smoke damage on the Nevada disclosure form
  • Get the parcel's floodplain status from the Assessor
  • Find out whether an unpermitted addition would need Washoe County Building review

Which office does what

Three county offices come into play when you sell, each at its own stage. Values, exemptions and appeals sit with the Assessor. Billing and collection belong to the Treasurer. Deed recording and transfer tax are the Recorder's job.

OfficeWhat it handlesContact
AssessorValues, tax cap status, exemptions, Board of Equalization appeals(775) 328-2277
TreasurerBills, collections, delinquent parcels, online payments775.328.2510, tax@washoecounty.gov, 1001 E 9th Street, Room D140, Reno
RecorderRecording deeds, Declaration of Value, transfer tax(775) 328-3661 for transfer tax questions

Phone payments are not accepted by the Treasurer, so use the website or the mail. Customer service answers Monday through Friday from 8am to 5pm.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Washoe County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Deadlines through the tax year

July 1 starts the county fiscal year, which ends June 30, and it is also the lien date. Apart from installment dates, these are the Assessor's milestones:

  • December 18: value notices reach owners
  • January 1: the real property roll closes
  • January 15: final day to appeal to the County Board of Equalization
  • March 10: final day to take a County Board ruling to the State Board
  • June 15: exemptions must be renewed or applied for, and rental owners file the tax cap form for the coming fiscal year
  • June 30: last day to contest a tax cap determination for the current year
  • July 5: exemption applications for property acquired after June 15 and before July 1

If January 15 lands on a weekend or holiday, the appeal can go in the next business day. The Treasurer mails bills by August 1, with payment due the third Monday in August, and any parcel with tax above $100 may pay in installments.

The 3 percent tax cap and a change of owner

What the cap restrains is the yearly rise in the bill. Assessed value itself is not capped. Assembly Bill 489, signed in 2005, sets 3 percent for a primary residence and a higher figure for other property. Certain rental dwellings can reach 3 percent as well. New construction, new parcels and parcels with a change in use come onto the roll without a cap.

In early May the county mails residential rental owners an affidavit, due back June 15. After an ownership change, non-rental property gets one too. Until a qualifying affidavit is on file, the parcel carries the higher general abatement. Appeals of a cap decision are answered within 30 days at (775) 328-2277. A buyer who will live in the house and files promptly can get 3 percent, whereas an investor buying a rental may land on a different cap. Raising it during the sale spares the buyer a shock on the first bill.

What happens to tax and transfer tax at closing

A lien attaches to each fiscal year's taxes on July 1. The Treasurer advertises parcels that go delinquent, and the owner has two years after the lien is filed to redeem by paying taxes, penalties and costs. Penalties are set by NRS 361.483.

Here is a detail that gets missed. Supplemental tax bills are not mailed to the mortgage company. If you are paying off a loan, find out whether a recent improvement or new construction triggered a supplemental bill.

Transfer tax is its own charge. Washoe County's rate is $2.05 on each $500 of value, the statewide $1.95 plus $0.10 locally. When the deed is recorded, the Recorder collects it based on the Declaration of Value. That value is the sale price or an estimated fair market value, drawn from the assessor's taxable value or a purchase within five years, whichever is higher. NRS 375.090 carves out transfers between former spouses under a divorce decree and transfers into a trust with no consideration.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Washoe County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What to bring when you call each office

A few items make every call shorter. Keep your parcel number handy, along with your most recent bill and the name on title. For the Assessor, have any notice of value, exemption paperwork and a note of when you bought. For the Treasurer, ask whether anything from an earlier year is open and whether a supplemental bill has been issued. For the Recorder, ask what documents must accompany the deed. Write down the date, the person you spoke with and the figure you were given, then pass it to the closing agent.

Owners with a rental should also ask about the tax cap form, since the June 15 deadline decides which cap applies for the next fiscal year.

Selling with taxes owed

Tax debt does not prevent a sale; it just has to be paid out of the deal. We buy Washoe County houses as-is, whether they are behind on taxes, inherited or rented. A written offer comes with no obligation if you say no.

A practical order of operations:

  1. Request the current tax balance from the Treasurer.
  2. Confirm your tax cap status with the Assessor.
  3. Ask the Recorder how the Declaration of Value works.
  4. Fill in the seller disclosure form at least 10 days before conveyance, which NRS 113.130 requires.
  5. Hand the payoff numbers to your closing agent so everything is cleared as the deed is recorded.

With cash, closing can be fast because no lender needs to sign off. Escrow subtracts the tax payoff from your proceeds just as it would a mortgage balance.

Frequently asked questions

Who collects property tax in Washoe County?

The Washoe County Treasurer. Bills go out by August 1, and the due date is the third Monday in August, with installments available when a parcel's tax is over $100. Phone payments are not taken.

When do I have to appeal my Washoe County assessment?

Appeal to the County Board of Equalization by January 15, or the next business day if it lands on a weekend or holiday. To challenge that board's decision, go to the State Board of Equalization by March 10.

What is the Washoe County transfer tax rate?

$2.05 per $500 of value, which is $1.95 statewide plus $0.10 for Washoe County. The Recorder collects it when the deed is recorded.

How does the 3 percent tax cap apply to a new buyer?

It limits the bill on a primary residence. After a sale the Assessor mails an affidavit, and the higher cap stays in place until a qualifying one is returned.

How long do I have to redeem a delinquent Washoe County parcel?

Two years from the date the lien is filed, by paying all taxes, delinquencies and costs. The parcel is advertised in the local newspaper, and the supplemental bill does not go to your mortgage company.

Lyon County in brief

Lyon County covers 2,024 square miles of western Nevada. Yerington is the county seat, and the communities include Fernley, Dayton, Silver Springs, Stagecoach, Smith Valley and Mound House, which sits on US 50 at the Carson City line. The 2020 count was 59,235 residents, with 74.7% of occupied homes lived in by their owners. Of 24,401 housing units, 7.0% stood empty.

Residents are split between town and country, with 55.4% living in urban areas and 44.6% in rural ones. For a seller that means a mix of subdivision homes, ranch parcels and raw land, each with its own buyer pool and its own paperwork.

Who handles property tax

The job is shared by three bodies. Value comes from the Assessor, billing from the Clerk-Treasurer, and the rate from the Nevada Tax Commission, which acts each spring on budgets submitted by local entities.

  • Assessor: 775-463-6520
  • Clerk-Treasurer: 27 S Main Street, Yerington, 775-463-6501
  • Recorder: 775-463-6581

The Assessor's job is to find taxable property, appraise it, and calculate 35% of the appraised amount as assessed value. The office sets no rate and collects nothing. Land is appraised at market value for its use. Structures are priced as if built new today, then marked down 1.5% each year, with a ceiling of 75%.

Market value has very little bearing on taxable value, especially as improvements age. Values can change every year, either through reappraisal or through factors the Tax Commission approves. Assessment notices reach owners with a changed value in December and June.

When is the tax due, and how do you pay it?

The bill comes once a year and is paid in four installments under NRS 361.483.

InstallmentDue date
FirstThird Monday of August
SecondFirst Monday of October
ThirdFirst Monday of January
FourthFirst Monday of March

A few practical points before a sale:

  • Mailing happens in mid to late July, right after the July 1 start of the fiscal year.
  • The county sends one bill to the address on file, or to the servicer when it has been told a servicer pays.
  • No bill goes out at each installment, and there are no reminders or payment confirmations.
  • Never getting a bill is not an excuse for paying late, so if early August passes with nothing in the mail, call for a reprint.
  • Each due date is followed by 10 days of grace.

Payment options are online (the QR code on the bill, or a parcel search on the county portal), by phone, in person at 27 S Main Street, by check in the drop box (no cash), or by mail to the Lyon County Treasurer. Penalties follow state law, from 4% for one late installment up to 7% for four.

How to appeal your assessment

Speak with the Assessor first. A filing with the County Board of Equalization is due January 15, shifting to the next business day if that is a weekend or holiday.

The county lays out the sequence this way:

  1. Go over the value with an appraiser, by phone or in the Assessor's Office.
  2. Submit the appeal to that office before January 15.
  3. Still unhappy? Take it to the State Board of Equalization.
  4. The courts come last.

Any of these bodies can adjust the assessed value, though none can touch a tax rate. The County Board has heard appeals in February, and its agendas list each one. Come with comparable sales, repair estimates and photos of anything that drags the home's worth down.

What the Recorder requires when a house sells

The Recorder wants a Declaration of Value with every transfer of title, which tells the office whether transfer tax is due or an exemption fits. Deeds, contracts of sale and some court orders all carry one. Copies of a recorded deed can be requested online, by phone or in person with advance payment.

The statewide transfer tax is $1.95 per $500 of value. Only Washoe, Churchill and Clark counties add more, so Lyon County sits at the base. The buyer and the seller are both liable, and payment happens as the deed is recorded. Some transfers are exempt, including transfers to or from a trust without consideration and a deed upon death under NRS 111.109.

The Recorder also keeps lien records, so a records search reveals anything recorded against a parcel. Owners can record a Declaration of Homestead for protection from involuntary liens. If an inherited house needs a death certificate, it comes from vital statistics in the state where the death occurred, not from the county.

Permit and building issues that slow a sale

Unpermitted work is the item that most often delays a Lyon County sale. The county's building rules cover these basics:

  • Small detached sheds (under 200 square feet, no electrical, mechanical or plumbing) need no permit. Bigger ones, or any with utilities, do.
  • Decks attached to a building need a permit. Detached decks under 200 square feet and less than 30 inches high do not, but must meet code.
  • Fences of seven feet or less need no permit, though front yard fences are limited to 3 feet.
  • Permits expire when work has not begun, or has stopped, for 180 days.
  • On a residential permit, the final signed inspection doubles as the certificate of occupancy.

Manufactured homes get extra scrutiny. They are allowed in most residential districts when no more than 6 years old at the time of the move, certified under the 1974 federal standard, and at least 1,200 square feet in more than one section. The county warns that unpermitted additions can impair future financing and sale. A failed septic leach field must be replaced under a county permit. In the Mason and Smith valleys, the Walker River Irrigation District must approve site plans. Power is not approved on vacant parcels, which matters when you sell raw land.

Before you contact a buyer

Collect your deed, the most recent tax bill and any records of permits for sheds, decks or additions. If the house sits on a septic system, locate the paperwork on the leach field. For an inherited property, order the death certificate from vital statistics in the state where the death occurred. Then call the Clerk-Treasurer for the current balance and ask which installments are still open. A seller who walks in with these items in hand can answer a buyer's first questions on the spot, and the title company can start its search without waiting.

Selling with tax due

Begin with the exact balance and the dates, then think about how quickly you must close. Unpaid tax is settled from the proceeds by the title company. Cash Home Buyers buys houses as-is and charges the seller no commission, no repair bills and no closing costs. Confirm every deadline, rate and fee with the Lyon County Assessor, Clerk-Treasurer and Recorder, since official pages change each fiscal year.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I pay property tax in Lyon County, Nevada?

Pay the Clerk-Treasurer, in person at 27 S Main Street in Yerington or by phone at 775-463-6501. Other choices are the online county portal, a check or money order mailed to the Lyon County Treasurer, and the drop box, which takes checks only.

When are Lyon County property tax installments due?

NRS 361.483 sets them at the third Monday of August and the first Mondays of October, January and March, with 10 days of grace after each.

What is the deadline to appeal a Lyon County property assessment?

January 15, or the next business day if it falls on a weekend or holiday. File with the Assessor's Office.

Does Lyon County assess property at market value?

No. The Assessor appraises land at market value for its use and buildings at replacement cost new less 1.5% depreciation per year, then takes 35% of that as assessed value. Market value has little bearing on taxable value as buildings age.

Do I owe transfer tax when I sell a house in Lyon County?

Usually. The Recorder collects $1.95 per $500 of value when the deed is recorded, and the buyer and seller share liability. A few transfers escape it, among them a deed upon death under NRS 111.109.

Selling in Carson City County? Get a Cash Offer

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Carson City County?

Is there a Carson City County?

Not in the usual sense. Carson City is a consolidated municipality: an independent city that also works as a county. A 1969 referendum folded the old Ormsby County into the city, and the legislature issued a new charter afterward. One government now covers both jobs, so the City Treasurer, City Assessor and City Recorder do what separate county offices would do elsewhere in Nevada. Hence the common search for a Carson City County tax guide.

The city spans about 157 square miles, starting in Eagle Valley and climbing west over the Sierra Nevada to the California-Nevada line in the lake. Reno sits roughly 30 miles north. Many houses near the Capitol are old, and buyers of those homes tend to ask about wiring, plumbing and additions made without permits.

Who to call for what

Because the city doubles as the county, three city desks stand in for the offices you would find elsewhere. Billing and payment sit with the Treasurer. The Assessor handles value, cap claim mailings and appeal petitions, reachable at (775) 887-2130. Deeds and transfer tax go through the Recorder at (775) 887-2000.

A quick call to each desk before listing can head off a late closing. The Treasurer can tell you where every installment stands. The Assessor can say if a cap claim is filed and whether recent building work reached the roll. The Recorder can list what must come with the deed.

Due dates and penalties

The yearly bill arrives in four pieces under Nevada law. Payment days are the third Monday of August, then the first Mondays of October, January and March, and each one comes with a 10-day grace window.

InstallmentWhen it is due
FirstThird Monday in August
SecondFirst Monday in October
ThirdFirst Monday in January
FourthFirst Monday in March

Two dates remain in fiscal year 2026/27: Monday, January 4, 2027 and Monday, March 1, 2027. The Treasurer posts the full schedule on the city's Treasurer page.

Mailing happens in July, to the owner's address in the Assessor's file. You get a bill even if your lender pays out of escrow, so confirm the lender really made the payment.

Each missed installment costs more than the last: 4% for the first, 5% for the second, 6% for the third, 7% for the fourth. Taxes left over from prior years grow by 10% a year, added monthly.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Carson City County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How does a tax sale work?

At the end of April, any parcel still owing is advertised in the local paper as delinquent. With three years unpaid, the Treasurer takes a trustee deed and may start a tax sale. City information says only a few parcels have gone to sale in the last fifteen years, so it is uncommon, but it does happen.

  • The notice cites NRS 361.565 and 361.570.
  • On the first Monday in June the Treasurer issues a certificate that holds the property subject to redemption.
  • The owner then has two years to redeem by paying the taxes, costs and 10% annual interest.

The amount shifts on each installment date. If you owe, get a current payoff before you list.

Tax cap, assessment and appeal dates

Nevada restrains how quickly a bill can climb. NRS 361.4723 holds an owner's primary residence, or a qualifying rental, to a 3% cap on the tax bill. Other property gets a higher cap that cannot go beyond 8%.

The Assessor publishes the higher cap year by year. It is 6.9% for 2026/27 and was 8.0% for each of 2022/23 through 2024/25. Property Tax Cap Claim forms go out on April 15 so owner-occupied houses can be sorted from rentals. A parcel with new construction or a change in use gets no abatement in the first year.

Notices of assessment arrive in late November. The appeal calendar looks like this:

  • January 15: last day to petition the County Board of Equalization.
  • January and February: that board hears appeals.
  • February and March: the State Board of Equalization meets.
  • June 30, 2027: last day to appeal a tax cap decision for 2026/27.

Petition forms are at the Assessor's office from December.

Recording and transfer tax

Each property transfer is taxable. Carson City's Recorder charges $3.90 per $1,000 of value, equal to the statewide base of $1.95 per $500, and wants a Declaration of Value filed with the deed. The Recorder's Office answers at (775) 887-2000.

At closing the title company fills in the form, collects the tax and prorates the installment under way. Request those figures in writing before signing day.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Carson City County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Steps when you sell with a tax balance

Owing tax does not stop a sale, though it sets the sequence. Start with the parcel's status from the Treasurer, including which installment is open and whether any older year is behind. Choose a closing date next, and have the title company divide the current installment between you and the buyer. The payoff then comes out of the sale money, with the remainder going to you.

If the house came to you through an inheritance, check how many installments have gone unpaid, because more than one missed payment means penalties stacking up while the paperwork is sorted.

Bring your deed, the latest tax statement, any cap claim paperwork and a payoff letter if there is a mortgage. Having these ready means the title company can order its search right away, and a buyer sees a seller who knows what is owed.

What a cash sale skips

Without a lender in the deal, nothing waits on loan approval or a bank appraisal. Clear title is still required, taxes and liens are still paid, and the deed still reaches the Recorder with its Declaration of Value. What drops away is the repair list a lender-backed buyer might demand, which matters for an older house with deferred work or additions nobody permitted.

What sellers in Carson City usually face

Most sellers run into timing and paperwork, not buyer demand.

  • An installment that comes due while the house is in escrow.
  • A tax cap claim that was never filed, or a claim tied to a rental that has since changed use.
  • Older homes with unpermitted work.
  • Inherited property with taxes unpaid across more than one installment.

Cash Home Buyers purchases houses as-is and can work around a tax balance, with the payoff paid from the sale. Whether you list or sell for cash, begin by pulling the parcel's tax status from the Treasurer.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Is there a Carson City County?

Not as its own government. Carson City is an independent city treated as a county equivalent since it merged with Ormsby County in 1969.

When are Carson City property taxes due?

Four installments: the third Monday in August, then the first Mondays of October, January and March, each with a 10-day grace period. The remaining 2026/27 dates are January 4 and March 1, 2027.

What is the late penalty in Carson City?

Penalties step up at 4%, 5%, 6% and 7% for the first through fourth late installments. Older delinquent taxes accrue 10% interest a year.

When is the appeal deadline for a Carson City assessment?

January 15 is the last day to petition the County Board of Equalization. That board sits in January and February, and the State Board follows in February and March.

How much is transfer tax in Carson City, and can I sell with delinquent taxes?

Transfer tax is $3.90 per $1,000 of value, with a Declaration of Value filed alongside the deed. A delinquent balance can be paid at closing, but taxes left unpaid for three years can lead to a trustee deed, so request a payoff early.

Clark County in brief

Nevada's southernmost county is also its biggest by population: 2,265,461 people in 2020, roughly 70% of the state, living on 8,061 square miles of land. Las Vegas is the seat. Henderson, North Las Vegas, Boulder City and Mesquite round out five incorporated cities, and 21 unincorporated towns fill in much of the rest.

Sellers should know one quirk. Over a million people in unincorporated areas still receive mail addressed to Las Vegas. Your property might fall under a city or under an unincorporated town, and that decides which planning, code and utility offices you work with. The county bills the tax in both cases.

Who handles property tax

Responsibility is divided three ways at the county. The Assessor determines value. The Treasurer sends the bill and receives the payment. The Recorder files the deed and collects transfer tax. Rates for each tax district come from the state Department of Taxation.

  • Treasurer mailing address: 500 S Grand Central Pkwy, Box 551220, Las Vegas, NV 89155-1220
  • Treasurer phone: (702) 455-4323, Monday through Thursday, 7:30 am to 5:30 pm; closed Friday through Sunday
  • Assessor appeals line: (702) 455-4997

Bills for real property go out once a fiscal year. Nothing in your mailbox by August 1? The automated phone system can send a copy. Under NRS 361.480, a bill that never came is not a defense for paying late. New owners who bought partway through the year, and owners whose lender quit paying, should call and ask for a bill.

Due dates and penalties

Payment of the whole bill is due on the third Monday in August. If the total exceeds $100 you can split it, though the county is clear that these are not quarterly payments. The split schedule runs August (third Monday), October, January and March (each first Monday). A 10-day window follows each date before any penalty attaches, and the penalty compounds as installments pile up:

Installments latePenalty on each late installment
One4%
Two9% on the first, 5% on the second
Three15%, 11% and 6%
Four22%, 18%, 13% and 7%

Homeowners with an escrow account should still verify that their servicer paid on time, since the county treats the owner as accountable. Email and text reminders can be set up through the Treasurer's page.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Clark County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Delinquency and tax auctions

By the end of April, parcels with unpaid tax are published as delinquent, both in the local paper and online at the Treasurer's site. A balance that survives to close of business on the first Monday in June puts the property into a two-year redemption period held by the Treasurer.

The owner buys the property back by paying taxes, accruing taxes, penalties and costs, with 10% interest per year from the original due date. A property found abandoned can be handled on a one-year track under NRS 361.567. If nobody pays, the deed goes to the County Treasurer acting as trustee, and the parcel can be put up at auction.

The county typically holds an auction at least yearly, often in spring, capping registration at 280 bidders and asking a $5,000 deposit. A property becomes eligible once it has been deeded to the trustee after three consecutive delinquent fiscal years, or two if it was abandoned.

You can still sell a house that is on a delinquent list before redemption ends. The closing pays off what is owed. The county keeps current rules on its real property tax page.

How is my home valued, and how do I appeal?

The cost method drives the Assessor's number. Staff estimate what it would take to rebuild the structure today, take off depreciation at 1.5% for each year of effective age (stopping at 50 years), then add what the land would sell for. The whole calculation is redone each year.

Because the rate depends on your tax district, your neighbor across a district line may pay differently. A home that qualifies for the 3% or 8% abatement pays whichever is lower, the calculated tax or the capped amount.

  • Forms: the Assessor has appeal forms in December.
  • Deadline: January 15, shifting to the next business day if it hits a weekend or holiday.
  • Next steps: if the County Board of Equalization agrees with the Assessor, you can go to the State Board, then to District Court.

Before filing, gather photos, repair quotes and recent sale prices of similar houses nearby. A call to the appeals line often settles a simple error without a hearing.

Transfer tax and recording

The Recorder collects $2.55 per $500 of value, counting a partial $500 as a full unit. The base is the full purchase price or estimated fair market value. Nevada's base rate is $1.95 per $500 statewide, and Clark County tacks on $0.60.

NRS 375.090 exempts certain transfers. Every deed needs a Declaration of Value, which the Recorder hands out free. An online calculator gives a rough figure, but your title company produces the final amount on the settlement statement.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Clark County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling with taxes owed

Tax debt gets settled at the table just as any lien would. The title company requests a payoff figure from the Treasurer, subtracts it from what you receive, and apportions the current installment between buyer and seller. If you are behind, check your parcel on the Treasurer's payment site first to see which installments are open.

Watch the calendar. A contract signed in September can run straight into the October installment, and each party owes a share of the year. If an escrow lender skipped a payment, correct that before closing day, because a surprise balance can stall the deal.

Collect your deed, your newest tax statement, a lender payoff letter if you have a mortgage, and any delinquency notice. Hand these to the title company early. A clean file shortens the wait between an accepted offer and the money in your account.

What Clark County sellers run into

Scale causes most of the trouble. A sale that works smoothly in one tax district can hit an unexpected snag in another, so confirm the details for your own parcel instead of assuming. Sellers who treat the Treasurer, Assessor and Recorder as three separate stops usually avoid the worst delays: one stop for the balance, one for any value dispute or abatement question, and one for the deed paperwork.

  • Rates differ by district, so you cannot copy a neighbor's bill.
  • An installment can fall due right after you sign.
  • Escrow lenders sometimes miss a payment.
  • Heirs may inherit a house with several unpaid installments.

Cash Home Buyers buys houses as-is anywhere in the county and can close around a tax balance, taking the payoff from the sale. We name no price until we have seen the property. For a first step, look up your parcel on the Treasurer's payment site and write down what is open.

Frequently asked questions

When are Clark County property taxes due?

Due in full on the third Monday in August. Bills over $100 can be paid across four dates instead, adding the first Mondays of October, January and March. Each date has a 10-day cushion.

What does a late payment cost in Clark County?

A single late installment adds 4%. Two late means 9% on the first and 5% on the second, and the percentages keep climbing at three and four.

What transfer tax applies in Clark County?

$2.55 for every $500 of value, built from the $1.95 state base plus a $0.60 county add-on.

How long do I have to appeal my assessment in Clark County?

File with the County Board of Equalization by January 15. Forms appear in December, and the Assessor's appeals line is (702) 455-4997.

Can I sell if my Clark County taxes are delinquent?

Yes, so long as the sale closes before redemption ends. What you owe in tax, penalties and interest is taken from the sale proceeds.

Where Douglas County sits

Douglas County lies in far western Nevada, stretching from the Carson Valley floor up the Sierra Nevada to the state line at Lake Tahoe. At 738 square miles only one Nevada county is smaller. Minden is the county seat, a title it took from Genoa in 1915.

No city or town here has been incorporated. Gardnerville, Gardnerville Ranchos, Minden, Genoa, Johnson Lane, Ruhenstroth, Indian Hills, Topaz Lake, Topaz Ranch Estates, Stateline and Zephyr Cove are all unincorporated, so county government handles parks, law enforcement, roads and building inspection for each. The same two offices, the Assessor and the Clerk-Treasurer, deal with a house in Stateline and a house in Gardnerville. No city tax desk exists to call.

The 2020 count was 49,488 residents, with 75.4% of occupied homes owner-occupied. The median age was 54.1 and 30.7% of residents were 65 or older. With nearly a third of the population at retirement age, sales by heirs are a regular part of this market, and an heir takes on the tax calendar together with the deed.

Who bills and who values

Billing and collection belong to the Clerk-Treasurer, while the Assessor deals strictly with value. Questions about rates or tax amounts belong with locally elected officials, as the county's own page puts it, and the Assessor's office cannot change them.

Fire and emergency medical service come from the Tahoe-Douglas Fire Protection District at the lake and the East Fork Fire Protection District across the rest of the county, and each adds its own levy to bills in its area. Nevada builds a bill from county, school, fire and other local levies by tax district, so two houses a few miles apart can carry different rates.

How the Assessor values a house

The Assessor starts with taxable value and takes 35% of it to get assessed value, the figure the tax rate is applied to. For a lot with a building, taxable value is the land at full cash value for its actual use plus the building's replacement cost new, less depreciation.

Depreciation runs at 1.5% per year of adjusted age, to a maximum of 50 years. As a result, market price connects to taxable value only loosely. The combined rate is capped statewide at $3.64 per $100 of assessed value, plus $0.02 for the state debt component, for a total of $3.66.

Two partial abatements limit how fast a bill can grow:

Property typeLimit on yearly increase in tax
Owner-occupied single-family primary residence3% over the prior year's tax
Other propertyGeneral abatement of up to 8%, set by a county formula using twice the CPI or a nine-year average of assessed value growth

Neither abatement covers property with no prior assessed value, property in its first year on the roll after new improvements, or property whose use has changed. If you remodeled recently or moved the house from rental to owner-occupied, test your situation against those exceptions.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Douglas County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How to appeal your assessment

Open with a call or a visit to the Assessor's office. The county reports that most questions end at the appraiser level, and the Assessor must hand over a copy of the latest appraisal within 15 days of your request. If that does not settle it, the formal path is:

  1. Ask the Assessor for the petition form, giving your name and the parcel number or street address.
  2. File one petition per parcel, or per parcel under different ownership, by January 15.
  3. Watch for written notice of the hearing date, sent at least ten days ahead.
  4. Attend the hearing. It is held under Nevada's Open Meeting Law and wraps up on or before February 28.

No attorney or accountant is required. Someone appealing for the owner needs a signed written authorization, and an attorney must be admitted to practice before the highest court of a state.

The Board looks at valuation only. It cannot change a tax rate or reduce a value because the owner is under financial strain. Further appeals go to the State Board of Equalization and then to the courts.

Selling with taxes owed

Money owed in tax comes out of the sale proceeds, and the title company gets the balance from the Clerk-Treasurer. Nevada bills real property in installments under NRS 361.483: the first falls on the third Monday of August, with later ones in October, January and March. After a ten-day grace period, penalties of 4%, 5%, 6% and 7% apply as one to four installments go unpaid.

A cash sale leaves the debt where it is and simply clears it faster. Get the payoff figure in writing and make sure it appears on the settlement statement.

Recording adds a cost of its own. Nevada's Real Property Transfer Tax is $1.95 for every $500 of value in every county, collected by the County Recorder when the deed is recorded. The buyer and seller are both on the hook, so the contract usually names the payer. The deed must be accompanied by a Declaration of Value. Exemptions cover transfers to or from a trust without consideration and a deed upon death under NRS 111.109, which matters when heirs are selling.

Preparing to sell

Line up the paperwork before you speak with any buyer. You will want the deed, the latest tax bill, the most recent appraisal if you asked the Assessor for one, and records of any remodel or addition. If heirs are involved, gather the documents showing who holds title. Ask the Clerk-Treasurer for the payoff, then let the title company order its own search so both numbers can be compared. An owner who shows up with complete records tends to close sooner than one who is still hunting for a lost bill the week before the signing.

What Douglas County sellers usually run into

Delays here usually come from timing, not weak demand. Typical examples:

  • An heir who lives out of state, has no local contact and needs a clear payoff from the Clerk-Treasurer.
  • A remodel or addition missing from the tax roll, so the abatement does not apply and the next bill jumps.
  • An owner who missed the January 15 appeal deadline and has to wait a full year to challenge a value.

Cash Home Buyers deals with owners in exactly these spots and buys houses as-is, no commission. A written offer is free, and declining it costs nothing. Confirm every deadline and figure with the Douglas County Assessor and Clerk-Treasurer before relying on it, because dates and rates shift each fiscal year.

Frequently asked questions

Who bills property tax in Douglas County, Nevada?

Billing and collection are the Clerk-Treasurer's job; valuation is the Assessor's. No cities are incorporated here, so these two offices cover everything from Gardnerville to Stateline.

What is the deadline to appeal a Douglas County assessment?

January 15, filed with the Assessor's office. Hearings wrap up by February 28, with at least ten days written notice.

Can the Board of Equalization lower my value because I cannot afford the tax?

No. The Boards weigh valuation only, not rates or tax amounts, and hardship is not a ground for a lower value.

Is there a cap on how much my Douglas County property tax can rise?

For most property, yes. Owner-occupied single-family primary residences are limited to a 3% increase, and other property to a general abatement of up to 8%. New improvements and a change in use fall outside the caps.

Can I sell a Douglas County house with unpaid property tax?

Yes. At closing the balance is paid from your proceeds, using a payoff quote from the Clerk-Treasurer. Penalties accumulate until then, so a quicker closing saves money.
